query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Thermomechanically processing a refractory high‐entropy alloy to develop a dual‐phase microstructure with homogeneous, coherent nanoprecipitates will improve its ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing its high strength or impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy intended for energetic structural applications.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical treatment—such as hot rolling followed by a calibrated annealing cycle—to induce a dual-phase structure featuring finely dispersed, coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Tests at ambient and dynamic (impact) loading conditions and at temperatures relevant to energetic material service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure in which coherent nanoprecipitates are uniformly distributed in the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates act as deformable obstacles that mitigate stress concentrations and promote more uniform dislocation motion, thereby enhancing ductility and uniform deformation while preserving mechanisms for high strength and the rapid release of stored energy under impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated (as-cast) alloy, the treated material will exhibit increased uniform elongation and enhanced deformability under impact, while retaining high yield and ultimate strength as well as the capacity for impact-induced energy release.
generation.baseline: The untreated as-cast single-phase alloy, which shows limited ductility and less uniform deformation under dynamic loading.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory high-entropy alloys used in energetic structural applications; however, its efficacy outside the defined temperature and strain rate regimes or in alloys with significantly different compositions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvements in ductility and uniform deformation, and the balance with energy-release properties, requires experimental validation; furthermore, scaling the treatment to different alloy systems or extreme service conditions may yield divergent results.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy sets from the same refractory high-entropy alloy composition: one as the untreated control and the other subjected to the proposed thermomechanical processing. Characterize both sets using microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) to verify the presence of coherent nanoprecipitates and perform standardized mechanical tests under quasi-static and dynamic (impact) conditions.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Uniform elongation and composite ductility metrics under impact
Energy release characteristics during high-strain rate loading (e.g., deflagration behavior)
TEM and/or other microscopy to confirm dual-phase microstructure with coherent nanoprecipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed alloy fails to show a statistically significant improvement in ductility and uniform deformability compared to the untreated alloy, or if there is any observed compromise in high strength or impact-induced energy release performance, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Design metastability in high-entropy alloys by tailoring unstable fault energies

Abstract: AbstractMetastable alloys with transformation-/twinning-induced plasticity (TRIP/TWIP) can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. Originated from the development of traditional alloys, the intrinsic stacking fault energy (ISFE) has been applied to tailor TRIP/TWIP in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) but with limited quantitative success. Here, we demonstrate a strategy for designing metastable HEAs and validate its effectiveness by discovering seven alloys with experimentally observed metastability for TRIP/TWIP. We propose unstable fault energies as the more effective design metric and attribute the deformation mechanism of metastable face-centered cubic alloys to unstable martensite fault energy (UMFE)/unstable twin fault energy (UTFE) rather than ISFE. Among the studied HEAs and steels, the traditional ISFE criterion fails in more than half of the cases, while the UMFE/UTFE criterion accurately predicts the deformation mechanisms in all cases. Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility). Doubled strength and ductility via maraging effect and dynamic precipitate transformation in ultrastrong medium-entropy alloy

Abstract: Demands for ultrahigh strength in structural materials have been steadily increasing in response to environmental issues. Maraging alloys offer a high tensile strength and fracture toughness through a reduction of lattice defects and formation of intermetallic precipitates. The semi-coherent precipitates are crucial for exhibiting ultrahigh strength; however, they still result in limited work hardening and uniform ductility. Here, we demonstrate a strategy involving deformable semi-coherent precipitates and their dynamic phase transformation based on a narrow stability gap between two kinds of ordered phases. In a model medium-entropy alloy, the matrix precipitate acts as a dislocation barrier and also dislocation glide media; the grain-boundary precipitate further contributes to a significant work-hardening via dynamic precipitate transformation into the type of matrix precipitate.
